title: The meal chant
hookLine: the reflection before eating: this food is for health, not for vanity

cards: Lunch at a monastery. The bowls are full, the food is warm, and everyone is hungry. Nobody starts eating.
Instead, the monks chant a few lines together in Pali, quietly, before the first bite. In a Zen hall the same pause happens with different words and wooden clappers.
To a guest it can look strange, sitting in front of good food and not eating it yet. But the pause is the point. Mostly, they're reminding themselves what eating is for.

teach.b: One source is in the Middle Length Discourses, in a teaching on how to let go of what clouds the mind. One of the ways is wise use, and food is one of the things used.

The Buddha says a monk reflects wisely as he eats: not for fun, not for intoxication, not for putting on bulk, not for looking good. Only to keep this body going, to ease the pangs of hunger, and to support the holy life.

teach.h: NOT FOR FUN, NOT FOR LOOKS.
teach.b: That's the thought behind today's line: for health, not vanity. In Theravada monasteries, a form of these words is still chanted at meals. Notice how unfussy it is.
It doesn't say food is bad, or the body is shameful, or eating is a sin. It says eat; just know why. Hunger is real, and food meets it.

But food can be pulled into other jobs: showing off, numbing out, comforting yourself after a bad day, turning a meal into a contest. The reflection doesn't scold any of that. It quietly puts food back in its place.
Zen communities have their own meal verses, which turn the same idea another way: considering the work that brought this food, and receiving it to support the practice.

teach.h: ONE BREATH BEFORE THE FIRST BITE.
teach.b: And then there's the pause itself, one breath before the first bite where you know what you're doing. For the Buddha, eating wisely was one way of guarding the mind.
A bowl of rice becomes a small practice at every meal, already built into your life.

how: In Theravada monasteries, monks recite a reflection on the purpose of food before eating, drawn from the Buddha's teaching on wise use; Zen communities chant their own meal verses before formal meals.

games.why: a few lines remind everyone what eating is for. the pause is part of the practice.

practice: Notice whether you're hungry right now, without changing it, and picture yourself sitting down to your next meal.
Before you pick anything up, say slowly, quietly or in your head, a reflection drawn from the Buddha's words: not for fun, not for looks, only to keep this body going. Then rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: The meal chant. The reflection before eating: this food is to keep the body going and support the practice, not for fun or looks. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali patisankha: reflecting wisely, the word the meal reflection begins with.

carryVoice: Your line: for health, not vanity. Food is welcome; the pause just remembers why. Eat well, and see you tomorrow.
